implementation_notes: Python has no constructor overloading, so the standard answer is one __init__ plus @classmethod alternative constructors that build the object from different raw material - exactly what datetime.date (today, fromtimestamp, fromisoformat, fromordinal), dict.fromkeys and pathlib.Path (cwd, home) do. A classmethod receives cls, so the alternative constructor still respects subclassing, and the classic private-constructor structure has no direct counterpart because Python has no access control: the 'private' part is convention (do not call __init__ directly) plus validation inside __init__ or in the alternative constructor itself.
pitfalls: There is no way to make __init__ inaccessible: a caller can always construct the object directly, so invariants must be enforced inside __init__ (or __new__) rather than trusting callers to use the alternative constructors.

A classmethod that must bypass __init__ has to use cls.__new__(cls) and initialize attributes itself - and still call the base initializer when the class is part of a cooperative hierarchy (or use singledispatchmethod).
Module-level factory functions (datetime.now) are idiomatic but carry no class, so subclasses cannot reuse them; prefer a classmethod whenever subclassability matters.
